text.html:
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease-MUC1 (ADTKD-MUC1) is part of a group of inherited disorders (collectively called autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease or ADTKD) that cause a slow loss of kidney function. People with ADTKD-MUC1 eventually develop kidney failure and need either dialysis to remove waste from the blood or a kidney transplant.

ADTKD-MUC1 causes kidney disease by impairing the kidneys' ability to filter waste products from the body and reabsorb nutrients back into the blood. Over time, this leads to kidney failure, which typically develops during mid-adulthood. However, the age at which kidney failure develops can vary greatly, even among members of the same family.

For people with ADTKD-MUC1, laboratory tests typically begin to indicate reduced kidney function in their late teens or early twenties. Unlike many other people with kidney disease, people with ADTKD-MUC1 typically do not have blood or protein in their urine. However, the initial signs of ADTKD-MUC1 can include:

• Increasing blood levels of creatinine, which is a waste product that is created when muscle tissue naturally breaks down
• Decreasing estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which is a measure of how well the kidneys are working

As ADTKD-MUC1 progresses, features of chronic kidney disease may appear:

• High blood pressure (hypertension)
• A low number of healthy red blood cells (anemia)
• High levels of a waste product called uric acid in the blood (hyperuricemia)
• A form of arthritis caused by a buildup of uric acid crystals in the joints (gout)

Occasionally, people with ADTKD-MUC1 have medullary cysts, which are fluid-filled pockets in the kidney that can be seen on an ultrasound or CT scan.
